entities.summary:
Muhammad ibn Yūsuf al-Warrāq, a pivotal Andalusían historian and geographer of the 10th century, stands as an indispensable source for understanding the Maghreb and al-Andalus during the height of the Caliphate of Córdoba. Born in an unknown location and dying on October 1, 973 CE, al-Warrāq dedicated his life to meticulously documenting the intricate political, social, and geographical landscapes of the western Islamic world. His magnum opus, *Kitāb Tartīb al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik* (Book of the Arrangement of Routes and Kingdoms), though surviving only in fragments and through the extensive citations of later scholars, offers a unique window into a crucial period of historical development.

Al-Warrāq’s methodology combined extensive travel with rigorous compilation of existing written sources, distinguishing him as a scholar of both direct observation and critical synthesis. He journeyed across North Africa, from the Atlantic coast to present-day Tunisia, documenting cities, trade routes, tribal affiliations, and local histories. His work provided unparalleled detail on the Berber tribes, the political structures of the Fatimid and Umayyad rivalries, and the economic life of major centers like Fez, Kairouan, and Sijilmassa. He meticulously recorded distances between settlements, geographical features, and the customs of diverse populations, creating a comprehensive survey crucial for both administrative and scholarly purposes.
